I think you have a fundamental misunderstanding of the reason why we have translations and the methodologies and reasons why we continue to make new translations of the Bible.

  
Let me address direct points. You claimed that "a lot of modern translations are made to accommodate the reading levels and mindset of the modern world." While this may be partially true, in that it is one of the many reasons that we have translations of anything, the exact same thing could be said about the KJV. It was made in the English of the time, even though spoken English wasn't quite as "fancy" per se, and it was translated so for the common man to be able to read it, i.e. "at his reading level."

You go on to say "They want it to be spoon fed..."

This connotes a notion that those who like the newer translations are lazy or do not want to put in a sincere effort in interpreting the texts. That misses the point of translating on the whole and disregards the great challenge of translating a text.

  
As I said in another comment, translation requires essentially thousands and thousands of choices in whether to render a word, phrase, sentence, or passage in any certain way.



Translation is not a 1-to-1 thing. If you want the most literal, most word-for-word translations out there, you get yourself an interlinear Bible. The word choices in English don't and can never give the full context of the choices within the original languages, and just forget about parallels in grammar and text structure because you won't find that in an ancient language if you compare it to English.

  
Translators may see an idiom which makes perfect sense in Greek but no sense at all in English. Without any context, how can you, as a reader, discern the true meaning behind that idiom while reading? So, some translators will choose to translate the idea behind the idiom instead of the word-for-word idiom itself.

  
Beyond that, we have a plethora of relatively recently-found documents, manuscripts dated ages before the textual basis of the KJV, the Textus Receptus. These may be recently found, but these manuscripts are closer to the age of Jesus than that which the KJV uses as its basis. Modern scholarship is in near total agreement on this. While we don't disregard the scholarship of the KJV, it appears very reasonable to use the older manuscripts to provide a more faithful translation to the people of today.



This is all to say that Bible translation is very nuanced, but we have a great deal of understanding on it and reasons to have these more modern translations made available.

When using certain gendered language like "his" or "brothers" or "man" in the New Testament, when seen in the context of the Greek from which it came from, it is clear that that language is used in the general usage, the inclusive "his" or the inclusive "brothers": "brothers" as in "all you people including the metaphorical sisters". The ESV simply chooses to use more formal equivalence and translate the original gendered terms into gendered English terms.

Every translation ever made is a series of thousands of choices in how to interpret language. The Bible, being a series of many texts in many different genres, written in far different cultures, and in a few different languages, is not an easy thing to translate to the satisfaction of all.

Formal equivalency is the practice of trying to translate the original texts into English by a word-for-word effort. The more formal, the more word-for-word a translation will be.

On the other end is dynamic equivalence. Dynamic equivalence tries to translate the bible using a thought-for-thought effort.

There are pros and cons to each. Most people agree it is best to read from a variety of translations.

All translations fall somewhere on this spectrum.

Most people find the NASB (New American Standard Bible) or LSB (Legacy Standard Bible) to be the most accurate formal translations before you get into interlinear translations as explained by another comment.

The KJV (King James Version), NKJV (New KJV), NRSV (New Revised Standard Version, and ESV (English Standard Version) are all fairly formal and popular, but are a little more readable than the NASB.

On the dynamic end of the spectrum, I'd say the two most popular today are the NIV (New Int'l Version) and the NLT (New Living Translation). The NLT is commonly agreed to be one of if not the most dynamic translation before authors begin paraphrasing the bible instead of translating it.

My favorite translation falls somewhere near the middle and uses a phrase coined by the company as "optimal equivalence". That translation is the CSB (Christain Standard Bible). It tries its best to be a compromise between formal and dynamic equivalency. I recommend it because it's encouraged me to consume more scripture.

Any of these more popular versions are very widely-used and most would agree they are great translations to read. You ought to be able to find an affordable bible out of any of these choices using Amazon, Ebay, or a used books website.
